sourcingNote:
This section goes further than the other culture topics: it is also about how people in Italy live, talk and behave, not only about rules.
So it has its own rule. A statement about people either rests on a statistic or an official source, or it is marked as common practice. Under a topic you find the sources and the date they are from. Where a topic has no source list, it describes common practice: it is not a survey result, and it varies by person, age and region. We write “many” or “most”, never “the Italians are ...”. About 59 million people live in Italy (ISTAT, 1 January 2026, provisional figure), and they are all different: young and old, from Lombardy to Sicily, from big cities and from villages. About 5.4 million of them have a foreign citizenship (ISTAT, as of 2026, provisional).
Where something is debated, both sides are shown. Rules and figures change; if in doubt, the linked official source is right.

topics.title: Saying hello: baci, handshake, Ciao / Buongiorno / Salve
topics.intro: In Italy, greeting is part of every meeting. Friends and family often give two kisses on the cheeks. At work and with new people, a handshake is normal. You also greet when you enter a shop or a lift, and you say goodbye when you leave.
topics.question: Come si saluta nel tuo paese? (How do people say hello in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age, the region and the place.

I baci: two light kisses on the cheeks, often just cheek to cheek. It is common between friends and family, between women, and between a woman and a man who know each other. Between men, a hug or a handshake is more usual.
At a first meeting, at work or with older people, a handshake (la stretta di mano) is the safe choice. You can say “Piacere” or “Molto lieto/a”.

“Ciao” is for friends, family, young people and people you use “tu” with. “Buongiorno” (morning and early afternoon) and “Buonasera” (from the afternoon or evening) are polite and always fine. “Salve” sits in between: not too formal, not too close.

When you enter a small shop, a bar, a waiting room or a lift, many people say “Buongiorno” to everyone. When you leave, they say “Arrivederci” or “Buona giornata”. “Ciao” as a goodbye also works with friends.
topics.context: If you are not sure whether to kiss, wait: most people show it with a small move towards you. A handshake is never wrong. Some people prefer not to kiss, and nobody should mind if you say so.
phrases: Buongiorno! (Good morning / Good day!)
Buonasera, come sta? (Good evening, how are you? Polite.)
Ciao, come va? (Hi, how is it going? Friendly.)
Piacere, mi chiamo Ana. (Nice to meet you, my name is Ana.)
Arrivederci e buona giornata! (Goodbye and have a good day!)

quiz.prompt: You meet your new boss for the first time. What is the safest greeting?
quiz.explain: A handshake is the safe choice at a first meeting at work.

quiz.prompt: Which greeting works for most people at any time of the day?
quiz.explain: Buongiorno and Buonasera are polite and fit nearly every situation. Ciao is for friends.

quiz.prompt: You enter a small shop with one other customer. What do many people do?
quiz.explain: Many people greet when they enter a shop and say goodbye when they leave.

topics.title: Queues and personal space
topics.intro: In Italy, people usually wait their turn, but the queue is often not a straight line. In many offices you take a number, and in a small shop or at the market you ask who is last. Some people also try to skip the line: they are called “furbi”. Many people stand closer than in some other countries and talk with their hands.
topics.question: Come si aspetta nel tuo paese? (How do people wait in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age, the region and the place.
At the post office, at the ASL and in many offices you take a ticket from a machine: “il numero da ritirare”. Watch the screen or listen for your number.
At the market, at the butcher or in a small shop without a ticket machine, ask “Chi è l’ultimo?” (Who is last?). Someone answers “Io”, and now you know who is before you.
A “furbo” (a smart one, with a negative tone) tries to skip the line. It is fine to say politely “Scusi, c’ero prima io” (Excuse me, I was here before).
Many people stand close in a queue or on the bus, and they may touch your arm when they talk. It is usually friendly. Bars and restaurants can be loud, and loud voices are not always an argument.
Gestures are part of the talk. Do not copy a gesture you do not understand: the same gesture can mean different things in different regions.
topics.context: If the line is unclear, ask “Chi è l’ultimo?” and say “Sono l’ultimo/a” to the next person. In a big office, look first for the ticket machine, often near the door.
phrases: Chi è l’ultimo? (Who is last?)
Io. / Sono io. (Me. / It is me. Said by the last person.)
Scusi, c’ero prima io. (Excuse me, I was here before.)
Permesso? / Posso passare? (May I? / Can I get past?)
Mi scusi. (Sorry. Polite.)

quiz.prompt: You come to a small shop with no ticket machine. What do you ask?
quiz.explain: You ask who is last, then you know when it is your turn.

quiz.prompt: What is “il numero da ritirare”?
options: A ticket with a number from a machine
quiz.answer: A ticket with a number from a machine
quiz.explain: In many offices you take a number and wait for it to be called.

quiz.prompt: Someone goes in front of you in the queue. What can you say politely?
quiz.explain: This sentence says politely that you were first.

topics.title: Please and thank you
topics.intro: In Italy, “per favore” and “grazie” are used a lot, and politeness also comes with a warm tone, a smile and “Lei”. Some phrases sound like a promise and are not: “ci vediamo” can mean “see you soon” or only “goodbye”.
topics.question: Quali parole gentili usi ogni giorno? (Which polite words do you use every day?)

table.label: What you say, and what it does
rows: Un caffè, per favore.
A normal, friendly order in a bar. Many people say “Buongiorno” first.
Grazie. / Grazie mille.
Thank you. “Grazie mille” is stronger, like “thanks a lot”.
Prego.
You are welcome. Also “please, go ahead” when you hold a door or offer a seat.
Mi scusi. / Scusa.
Excuse me or sorry. “Mi scusi” is polite (Lei), “scusa” is for friends (tu).
Magari.
“I wish!” or “maybe”. The tone shows if it is yes or a soft no.
Ci vediamo.
See you. It can be a real plan or only a nice goodbye. Ask “Quando?” if you want a date.

facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age, the region and the place.

“Lei” is the polite form of “you” for one person, with the third person of the verb: “Come sta?” (How are you?). It is normal with strangers, older people, officials and in many jobs. “Tu” is for friends, family, children and many young people. If you are unsure, start with “Lei” and wait for “Diamoci del tu”.
“Prego” has many uses: “you are welcome”, “please come in”, “after you”. In a shop, “Prego?” can mean “What would you like?”.
Many people say “per favore” or “per piacere” when they ask, and “grazie” when they get something. In a bar, people often say “Grazie, buona giornata” when they leave.
“Magari”, “vediamo” and “ci penso” can be a polite way not to say no. Check the tone and ask again if you need a clear answer.
topics.context: Italian often softens requests with “potrebbe” (could you) or “le dispiace se…?” (do you mind if…?). You do not need long sentences, but a polite word before the question helps.
phrases: Un caffè, per favore. (A coffee, please.)
Grazie mille! (Thanks a lot!)
Prego, si accomodi. (You are welcome, please sit down.)
Potrebbe ripetere, per favore? (Could you repeat, please?)
Diamoci del tu? (Shall we use “tu”?)

quiz.prompt: A shop assistant says “Prego?” to you. What does she mean?
quiz.explain: In a shop “Prego?” means “Can I help you?”.

quiz.prompt: A new colleague says “Ci vediamo!”. What does it often mean?
quiz.explain: It can be a real plan or only a goodbye. If you want a date, ask “Quando?”.

quiz.prompt: You speak to an older stranger. Which form is the safe choice?
quiz.explain: “Lei” is the polite form for one person and the safe start.

topics.title: Time and timing
topics.intro: In Italy, times at work, at the doctor and for trains are fixed, and you should be on time. For a meal with friends, a party or a visit, many people come ten to fifteen minutes late, and the host expects this. In the south, “subito” can mean “in a moment” and not “right now”.
topics.question: Quanto è importante essere puntuali nel tuo paese? (How important is being on time in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age, the region and the place.
For a job interview, an office appointment, the doctor, a train or an exam, be on time or a bit early. If you are late, call or write.
For an invitation at home, many people arrive 10 to 15 minutes after the time. If the host says “alle otto”, you do not need to ring the bell at 20:00 sharp.

Meal times are later than in many countries. Many people have lunch (pranzo) around 13:00 and dinner (cena) around 20:00 or later, and in the south often later still. Many restaurants open for dinner at 19:30 or 20:00.
“Subito” (at once) and “tra poco” (in a short time) can be loose. “Un attimo” (a moment) can last a few minutes. If it is important, ask “Quando, più o meno?”.
Many shops and offices close for a break at lunch, and the hours differ by city and by region. Check the opening hours online or on the door.
topics.context: If you are late for a social meeting, a short message is polite: “Sto arrivando, faccio tardi di dieci minuti.” For a formal appointment, say sorry as soon as you arrive: “Mi scusi per il ritardo.”
phrases: Sono in ritardo, scusami. (I am late, sorry.)
Sto arrivando! (I am on my way!)
Alle otto, più o meno. (At eight, more or less.)
A che ora aprite? (When do you open?)
Mi scusi per il ritardo. (Sorry for being late. Polite.)

quiz.prompt: You have a doctor’s appointment at 10:00. When do you arrive?
quiz.explain: For a doctor, an office or an interview, be on time.

quiz.prompt: A friend invites you for dinner at 20:00. What is common?
quiz.explain: At private meals a short delay is normal and often expected.

quiz.prompt: Someone says “subito”. What may it mean?
options: In a moment, not always at once
quiz.answer: In a moment, not always at once
quiz.explain: “Subito” can be loose. Ask again if you are in a hurry.

topics.title: Paying the bill
topics.intro: In Italy, one person often says “offro io” (it is on me) for a coffee, an aperitivo or a round. In a restaurant, many groups split the bill equally, “alla romana”, and others ask for separate bills. You may also see “il coperto” (cover charge) on the bill.
topics.question: Come si paga al ristorante nel tuo paese? (How do people pay in a restaurant in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age, the region and the place.
“Offro io” means “I pay”. It is a friendly gesture, and you can pay the next round. Do not argue for a long time, say “Grazie, la prossima volta offro io”.
“Alla romana” (“facciamo alla romana”) means that everybody pays the same share. It is easy but not always fair if you ate and drank less. You can say “Preferisco pagare il mio”.
In many bars, people pay at the till (la cassa) first, get the receipt (lo scontrino) and show it at the counter. In others you pay after the coffee. Look at what others do.
“Il coperto” is a fixed charge per person in many restaurants. It must be shown on the menu and on the bill. It is not a tip. Tipping is not required, and a small round-up is a kind gesture.
“Il caffè sospeso” is a tradition from Naples: you pay a coffee for a stranger. It is not found everywhere, and it is not a rule.
topics.context: If you want to pay separately, say it at the start of the meal or when you ask for the bill: “Il conto separato, per favore”. Many places can do it, some prefer not to.
phrases: Il conto, per favore. (The bill, please.)
Offro io! (It is on me!)
Facciamo alla romana? (Shall we split equally?)
Paghiamo separatamente. (We pay separately.)
C’è il coperto? (Is there a cover charge?)

quiz.prompt: What does “facciamo alla romana” mean?
quiz.explain: The bill is divided equally between all people.

quiz.prompt: What is “il coperto”?
quiz.explain: It is a charge per person for the table and the bread. It is not a tip.

quiz.prompt: A friend says “Offro io”. What can you answer?
options: Grazie, la prossima volta offro io.
quiz.answer: Grazie, la prossima volta offro io.
quiz.explain: You accept and offer the next round.

topics.title: Small talk and the aperitivo
topics.intro: In Italy, many people meet and talk in a bar, at an aperitivo before dinner, or on an evening walk, la passeggiata. Small talk is easy with food, family, football and the weather. “Come va?” is a greeting, not always a real question.
topics.question: Di cosa si parla con persone nuove nel tuo paese? (What do people talk about with new people in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the group, the age and the place.

L’aperitivo is a drink and often small snacks, usually in the early evening. In some cities, such as Milan, bars offer a big buffet with it. It is a normal way to meet friends or colleagues, and it is not a full dinner.
Many people have a coffee at the bar counter, “al banco”, and talk with the barista or neighbours for a minute. A bar is a place for short, friendly chats.
La passeggiata is an evening walk in the town centre, especially in small towns and in the south. People walk, meet and talk. It is a social habit, not a sport.
“Come va?” and “Tutto bene?” are common greetings. The usual answer is short: “Bene, grazie, e tu?”. A long answer about problems is not expected.
Safe topics: food, where you are from, travel, work, family, football and the place you live. Many people avoid strong opinions about politics, religion or money with people they do not know well.
topics.context: Questions about family, children or work can sound personal, but they are usually interest and not a test. You can answer short, or say “Preferisco non parlarne” (I prefer not to talk about it).
phrases: Di dove sei? (Where are you from?)
Che lavoro fai? (What do you do?)
Prendiamo un aperitivo? (Shall we have an aperitivo?)
Tifi per qualche squadra? (Do you support a team?)
Com’è il tempo da te? (What is the weather like where you are from?)

quiz.prompt: When is an aperitivo usually?
quiz.explain: It is a drink and a snack before dinner.

quiz.prompt: Someone asks “Come va?” in passing. What is a good answer?
options: A long story about your week
quiz.explain: It is mostly a greeting, a short answer is normal.

quiz.prompt: What is la passeggiata?
options: A walk in the evening to meet people
quiz.answer: A walk in the evening to meet people
quiz.explain: It is a social walk in the town centre.

topics.title: Making friends
topics.intro: In Italy, family is at the centre for many people, and friendships often come from school, the neighbourhood, work, a sport or an association. New friendships can take time, but people are often open once they know you. In an apartment building, the condominio group on WhatsApp is a common first contact.
topics.question: Come si fanno amicizie nel tuo paese? (How do people make friends in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age, the region and the place.

Many people keep friends from school and from their home town for life, and family often comes first at the weekend. It can feel closed at first. A repeated invitation, such as a coffee, is a good sign.

In many apartment blocks, the residents have a WhatsApp group for the condominio, with messages about meetings, noise, repairs and the lift. Read it, be polite and do not take every message personally.
Associations are a good way to meet people: sports clubs, choirs, parish groups (oratorio), volunteering (volontariato) and the pro loco in small towns.
“Ci sentiamo” (we will be in touch) and “ci vediamo” are friendly, but they are not always a plan. If you want to meet, suggest a day: “Sabato prendiamo un caffè?”.
Many people like to invite friends home or to a Sunday lunch with the family. If you are invited, bring a small gift, for example dessert or flowers.
topics.context: Be the one who suggests a plan. Many people answer “volentieri” (gladly) if they mean yes.
phrases: Ci sentiamo! (We will be in touch!)
Sabato prendiamo un caffè? (Shall we have a coffee on Saturday?)
Volentieri! (Gladly!)
Vuoi venire a pranzo da noi? (Do you want to come for lunch at ours?)
Posso unirmi al gruppo? (Can I join the group?)

quiz.prompt: What is the condominio group on WhatsApp usually about?
options: News about the building: meetings, repairs, noise
quiz.answer: News about the building: meetings, repairs, noise
quiz.explain: It is for the people who live in the same building.

quiz.prompt: A new friend says “Ci sentiamo”. What do you do if you want to meet?
quiz.explain: The phrase is friendly but often not a plan. Suggest a day.

quiz.prompt: What is a good way to meet people?
quiz.explain: Associations, clubs, the oratorio and volunteering bring people together.

topics.title: How hiring works
topics.intro: In Italy, a personal contact can help to find a job: “una raccomandazione” or “le conoscenze”. Many jobs are also found by CV, online and through the Centro per l’impiego. After the interview (il colloquio), there is often a trial period. Work “in nero”, without a contract, is illegal.
topics.question: Come si trova lavoro nel tuo paese? (How do people find work in your country?)
facts: This describes common practice and the general rules. It is not legal advice, and it changes with the sector and the region.
“Una raccomandazione” is a recommendation from a person with a contact. It can open a door. It is debated, because many people see it as unfair to those without a network.

A CV (il curriculum) is usually 1 or 2 pages. The Europass format is known. A photo is not required, and the law does not allow discrimination by age, sex or origin. Some applicants add a short “lettera di presentazione”.
The interview is called “il colloquio”. Ask about the contract type, the CCNL (national collective agreement) and the pay (RAL, gross annual salary).
“Il periodo di prova” is a trial period written in the contract. Its maximum length depends on the CCNL and the law. Read the contract before you sign.

“Lavoro in nero” is work without a contract and without social contributions. It is illegal and leaves you without protection. Ask for a written contract before you start, and ask the Centro per l’impiego, a union or an official office if in doubt.

pros: A personal contact can open a door, and a tip from a friend is quick.
A clear CV is easy to read and to compare.
Small firms can answer fast and decide after one talk.
cons: People without a network in Italy can feel left out.
Some employers may treat people differently by age, name or origin, although the law forbids discrimination.
The trial period and the contract type can be unclear if you do not read the contract.

topics.context: Always ask for the contract in writing, and keep a copy. If someone offers work “in nero”, you can ask a union (sindacato) or the Ispettorato del lavoro for general orientation.
phrases: Sto cercando lavoro nel settore della ristorazione. (I am looking for work in hospitality.)
Le invio il mio curriculum. (I am sending you my CV.)
Che tipo di contratto è? (What kind of contract is it?)
Quanto dura il periodo di prova? (How long is the trial period?)
Quale CCNL si applica? (Which collective agreement applies?)

sources.label: Ministero del Lavoro e delle Politiche Sociali

quiz.prompt: What is “il colloquio”?
quiz.explain: Il colloquio is the talk with the employer.

quiz.prompt: What is “lavoro in nero”?
quiz.explain: It has no contract and no contributions. Ask for a written contract.

quiz.prompt: What is “il periodo di prova”?
options: A trial period in a new job
quiz.answer: A trial period in a new job
quiz.explain: It is written in the contract and has a maximum length.

topics.title: Cars, trains and getting around
topics.intro: In Italy, how you travel depends on where you live. In big cities many people use metro, bus and tram. Between cities the fast trains of Trenitalia (Frecciarossa) and Italo are popular. In smaller places a car is often needed. ZTL zones, motorway tolls and strikes are part of daily life.
topics.question: Come ti muovi nella tua città? (How do you get around in your city?)
facts: Trenitalia runs regional trains (regionale) and fast trains (Frecciarossa, Frecciargento, Intercity). Italo is another company with fast trains. Regional trains are cheaper and slower.

For regional trains with a paper ticket, you must validate it (convalidare) at the small machine on the platform before you board. With a ticket on your phone, check the rules of the company. A ticket that is not validated can lead to a fine.

The ZTL (zona a traffico limitato) is a zone in many city centres that you may enter only with a permit or at certain hours. Cameras read the number plate, and a fine can arrive weeks later, also for hire cars. Look for the sign “ZTL attiva”.

On the autostrada, you take a ticket at the entrance and pay the toll (il pedaggio) at the exit, with cash, card or Telepass. Telepass is a device for automatic payment. The general speed limit on motorways is 130 km/h unless signs say otherwise.
A “sciopero” (strike) can stop trains, buses and flights for some hours or a day. The dates are announced in advance. Check the company site or the news before an important trip.

The blood alcohol limit for drivers is 0.5 g/l, and 0 for novice drivers (first years), drivers under 21 and professional drivers. Check the official rules. The driving licence (patente) is covered in the patente vocabulary.

prosCons.prosLabel: Why many people like the car
pros: It is flexible for villages, shift work and trips with children.
In many regions, public transport is rare outside the big towns.
It saves time on routes without a direct train.
prosCons.consLabel: Why many people prefer trains and public transport
cons: Parking, fuel, tolls and ZTL fines cost money.
In big cities, metro and bus are often faster than the car.
A train lets you read or work on the way.

topics.context: Before you drive into a city centre, look for ZTL signs, or ask your hotel or the Comune. For a long trip, compare train and car, and check strike dates.
phrases: Un biglietto per Firenze, per favore. (A ticket to Florence, please.)
Da quale binario parte il treno? (Which platform does the train leave from?)
Devo convalidare il biglietto? (Do I have to validate the ticket?)
C’è uno sciopero domani? (Is there a strike tomorrow?)
Dove posso parcheggiare qui? (Where can I park here?)

sources.label: Ministero delle Infrastrutture e dei Trasporti

quiz.prompt: You have a paper ticket for a regional train. What must you do?
options: Validate it at the machine before boarding
Show it only at the exit
quiz.answer: Validate it at the machine before boarding
quiz.explain: Without validation you may get a fine. Check the rules for e-tickets.

quiz.prompt: What is the ZTL?
options: A zone in the city centre with limited access
quiz.answer: A zone in the city centre with limited access
quiz.explain: Entering without a permit can lead to a fine from the camera.

quiz.prompt: What is Telepass?
options: A device to pay motorway tolls automatically
quiz.answer: A device to pay motorway tolls automatically
quiz.explain: You can also pay the pedaggio with cash or card.

topics.title: Women and men at work
topics.intro: In Italy, women and men have equal rights by law, but the numbers show differences at work, for example in employment rates and in who stays home with children. Parental leave exists for mothers and fathers, and people debate how well it works. This topic stays with facts and sources.
topics.question: Com’è la situazione nel tuo paese? (What is the situation in your country?)
facts: The employment rate of women aged 20 to 64 in Italy is lower than that of men and lower than the EU average (ISTAT and Eurostat: around 57% for women and 76% for men in 2024, to verify). The gap is larger in the south.

“Il congedo di maternità” is compulsory leave of five months around the birth. Fathers have a compulsory leave of 10 working days and can take more through “il congedo parentale” (as of 2026, details to verify with INPS).

At marriage, a woman keeps her own surname by law. She may add her husband’s name in some documents. Since 2022, a decision of the Constitutional Court lets children take both parents’ surnames (to verify the current rule).

Titles: “signora” is used for women in general, “signorina” is now rare and can sound old-fashioned. People use “dottore / dottoressa” for a graduate, and also for many professionals. Use the title that the person uses.
Women and men share the same labour laws, the CCNL and the right to equal pay. The “Consigliera di parità” deals with discrimination at work (to verify).

prosCons.prosLabel: What many people point to as progress
pros: Both parents have a right to leave, which supports shared care.
Public data on pay and employment makes the debate more factual.
Surname rules treat mothers and fathers alike on paper.
prosCons.consLabel: What many people say is still open
cons: The employment gap between women and men remains, mostly in the south.
Care work still falls more often on women.
People disagree about the reasons and about the best measures.

topics.context: If you think you were treated unfairly at work, you can ask a union (sindacato), the Consigliera di parità or the Ispettorato del lavoro. This is general orientation, not legal advice.
phrases: Vorrei informazioni sul congedo parentale. (I would like information about parental leave.)
Sono la dottoressa Rossi. (I am Dr Rossi.)
Il suo cognome è Bianchi. (Her surname is Bianchi.)
Ho diritto a un congedo? (Am I entitled to leave?)
A parità di lavoro, parità di stipendio. (Equal pay for equal work.)

quiz.prompt: What happens to the surname of a woman who marries, by law?
quiz.explain: The law lets her keep her surname. She may add the husband’s name in some documents.

quiz.prompt: Who can take leave after a birth?
quiz.explain: Both have rights, with different rules for length.

quiz.prompt: Which title is common for a woman with a university degree?
quiz.explain: “Dottoressa” is a very common title for a graduate.

topics.title: Dating basics
topics.intro: In Italy, a first date is often just “uscire” (going out) for an aperitivo or a coffee. Many people use apps, but also meet through friends and family. The words “fidanzato/a” and “ci frequentiamo” show the stage of a relationship. Meeting the family is a bigger step than in some other countries.
topics.question: Come funzionano gli appuntamenti nel tuo paese? (How does dating work in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age, the region and the place.
“Uscire con qualcuno” means to go out with someone. “Ci vediamo per un aperitivo?” is a normal first invitation. It is light, not a promise of a relationship.
Many people meet through dating apps, friends, work or events. The first meeting is usually in a public place, such as a bar. Tell a friend where you are.
“Fidanzato/a” means boyfriend or girlfriend, and often a serious relationship. “Ci frequentiamo” means “we are seeing each other” and is less strong. “Stiamo insieme” means “we are together”.
Paying: one person may say “offro io”, or you split. Do not feel obliged to pay for the other. It is fine to say “Facciamo a metà” (let’s split).
Meeting the family, for example for Sunday lunch, usually comes later and is a sign that it is serious. Bring a small gift.
topics.context: A no is a no, in every country. If you are not sure what the other person means by a vague phrase, ask kindly and directly: “Ti va di rivederci?” (Would you like to see each other again?)
phrases: Ti va di uscire sabato? (Would you like to go out on Saturday?)
Ci vediamo per un aperitivo? (Shall we meet for an aperitivo?)
Mi sono divertito/a molto. (I had a great time.)
Siamo fidanzati. (We are a couple.)
Facciamo a metà? (Shall we split?)

quiz.prompt: “Ci vediamo per un aperitivo?” is...

topics.title: Direct and indirect
topics.intro: In Italy, many people talk with their hands and with a warm tone, and a clear “no” is often softened. People say “magari”, “vediamo” or “non so” when they may mean no. A direct question is not rude, but a polite frame helps. Between friends and at home, people can be very direct.
topics.question: Quanto sono diretti i dialoghi nel tuo paese? (How direct is talk in your country?)

table.label: Direct and softer forms
rows: Dammi un caffè.
Mi dai un caffè, per favore? / Vorrei un caffè.
No.
Magari un’altra volta. / Purtroppo non posso.
Hai torto.
Non sono sicuro che sia così. / Io la vedo diversamente.
Non mi piace.
Non è proprio il mio genere. / Ma anche no.
Voglio parlarti.
Hai un attimo? Vorrei dirti una cosa.
Pagami.
Scusa se ti disturbo, quando riesci a mandarmi i soldi?

facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age, the region and the place.

A soft no: “Magari!” can mean “I wish” or “perhaps”. “Vediamo” (we will see) and “Ci penso” (I will think about it) can mean “probably not”. Ask a clear question if you need an answer: “Posso contare su di te?”.
“Ma anche no” (but also no) is a light, humorous, almost polite no, used among friends.
Gestures help the meaning: a shrug shows “who knows”, a hand with joined fingers can show a question. Gestures differ by region, and some can be rude in another country.
At work, requests often come with “se possibile”, “quando hai un attimo” or “potresti…?”. These are soft but still real requests.
People do give direct opinions, for example about food, football or family, and a loud discussion is often not a fight.
topics.context: If you must say no, give a short reason and a polite tone: “Purtroppo non posso, grazie lo stesso”. If you need a clear answer from the other person, ask in a friendly way: “Quindi è un sì o un no?”
phrases: Magari un’altra volta, grazie. (Maybe another time, thanks.)
Purtroppo non posso. (Unfortunately I cannot.)
Ci penso e ti faccio sapere. (I will think and let you know.)
Ma anche no! (Well, not really!)
Scusa, non ho capito bene. Intendi di sì? (Sorry, I did not understand well. Do you mean yes?)

quiz.explain: It is a light and funny no among friends.

topics.title: Humour and banter
topics.intro: In Italy, many friends tease each other, “si prendono in giro”, and a bit of irony is part of daily talk. A joke can be local, with dialect, and not every topic is funny. You may hear “scherzi a parte” when someone turns serious.
topics.question: Che tipo di umorismo c’è nel tuo paese? (What kind of humour is there in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age, the region and the place.
“Prendere in giro” means to tease someone in a friendly way. It often shows that people like you. If it hurts, you can say “Dai, smettila” (Come on, stop).
Irony and sarcasm are common. People sometimes say the opposite of what they mean, with a tone and a smile. If you are not sure, ask “Dici sul serio?” (Do you mean it?).
“Scherzi a parte” (jokes aside) is used to switch to a serious topic. “Scherzavo” means “I was joking”.
Many regions have their own dialect and jokes about neighbouring towns or regions. These jokes are usually told by locals. As a visitor, wait before you make them.
Careful topics: religion, death, politics and people’s families, if you do not know the group well. Jokes about weight, looks or origin can hurt.

prosCons.prosLabel: What many people like about banter
pros: It can make a group closer and the talk lighter.
It shows trust: people tease those they like.
cons: Irony is hard to read in a second language.
A joke can hurt without intention.
Some people prefer less teasing, and that should be respected.

topics.context: If you are the target of a joke and it is not nice, say it calmly: “Non mi fa ridere”. Among friends, this is usually accepted.
phrases: Dai, stai scherzando! (Come on, you are joking!)
Scherzi a parte, ho un problema. (Jokes aside, I have a problem.)
Scherzavo! (I was joking!)
Dici sul serio? (Do you mean it?)
Non mi fa ridere. (It does not make me laugh.)

quiz.prompt: What does “prendere in giro” mean?
quiz.explain: It is usually friendly but should not hurt.

quiz.prompt: What is “scherzi a parte” used for?
options: To say that you now speak seriously
quiz.answer: To say that you now speak seriously
quiz.explain: It means “jokes aside”.

quiz.prompt: Which topic is better to avoid in a joke with people you do not know?
quiz.explain: These topics are personal and can hurt.
